name: Midnight
lede: Midnight is the color of the sky at its darkest, a name that books use for deep indigo blues, and the swatch here is a near-black navy that few painters ever needed.

sections.title: A time of day as a color
sections.body:
St Clair's glossary defines midnight as the dark blue of the night sky [1]. Paterson lists *midnight blue* as an intense blue, apparently the correct shade for men's evening dress [2]. Midnight and midnight blue are not the same swatch in our data: the ISCC-NBS 1955 entry for Midnight is a dark purple, while the near-black navy here comes from the xkcd color list [3].

Garfield's account of the English color vocabulary counts about 7,500 names, of which 55 come from times of day, with midnight blue as his example [4]. The name has a surprising rival: *midnight sun*, in the Pigment Compendium, is a synonym of chrome scarlet, a red [5]. In the Goethe-Schiller *Temperamentenrose* of the late 1790s, red itself stood for midnight, among air, north, winter and old age [6].

sections.title: The midnight of indigo
sections.body:
The blue most often called midnight in the books is indigo. Balfour-Paul recalls a cloth lifted from the vat and watched as it turned from yellow through turquoise to midnight blue in the air [7]. West African dyers embroidered cloth, dyed it and removed the threads, leaving pale patterns like ghosts on a ground like a midnight sky [8]. Chinese and Korean Buddhist sutras of the ninth to fifteenth centuries were written in gold and silver on indigo paper, burnished with agate until it turned lustrous midnight blue [9]. Midnight blues were also favored in the Islamic courts, beside crimson from insect dyes [10].

Newton is part of this story. Finlay says he added indigo to the spectrum, probably to reach seven, and that indigo was then chiefly a dye word, which is why the midnight stripe is hard to find in a real rainbow [11]. Finlay also reports that Binney & Smith renamed its Prussian blue crayon Midnight Blue in 1958, after teachers said children could not relate to Prussian history [12]. See [[midnight-blue]] and [[prussian-blue]] for those two.

sections.title: Midnight in paint
sections.body:
Ball's chapter on blue is titled *Shades of Midnight*, and he describes the dark blues that clothe the figures of Picasso's *The Absinthe Drinker* and *Old Woman*, both of 1901, as midnight blues [13]. Even those are lighter than the swatch here, which is only a few steps from black.

On a screen the swatch is easy to mistake for black, and its blue shows only beside a true black [3]. For the learnable color nearest to it, see [[oxford-blue]].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in only 10 works [14]. Every one is a shadow area, never a mid-tone or light [14]. The earliest is Fra Angelico's *Madonna and Child with Four Angels*, of 1420, at 12.4 per cent [14]. The largest are Huntington's portrait *Dr. James Hall*, of 1857, at 42 per cent, and Paudiß's *The Head of a Girl*, of 1653, at 37 per cent [14].

By century the clearest signal is the 1700s, with 5 of 3,449 works, 3.5 times the archive rate, and British paintings carry 4 of 593 [14]. Old varnish and soot darken blues in these pictures, so some may be darker now than they were painted, and a match to the screen is not a pigment test [14].

In print, *midnight blue* is almost absent before 1900 and reaches about 46 per cent of its 2015 peak by 1940 [15].
